lesson_title: Profitable and Broke: Cash Budgets and Projected Income Statements
hook_text: Record month. Empty account. Both true — here's how.
clip_script: Your brother washes cars on weekends. In June he washes sixty cars at R150 each — R9 000 of work, his best month yet. Ask him how June went: excellent. But a third of his customers said "sort you out at month end". So on the thirtieth he's holding R6 000 in cash and R3 000 in promises. Did he EARN well? Yes — R9 000, the work is done. Can he buy a pressure washer on the first? Only R6 000 says yes. Two truthful answers about one month — and that's why a business runs TWO forecasts. One predicts what the months will earn. One predicts what the bank will actually hold. Now scale it up: a shop posts its record month, R280 000, mostly on credit. The stock was paid for in May. Wages went out. The owner bought a delivery scooter for cash. And the customers who owe R140 000? They pay in July. The account hits zero in the month the shop broke its own record. Profit measures whether a business deserves to survive. Cash decides whether it does.
visual_style: A driveway car-wash bucket filling with coins beside a stack of IOU notes; then a shop's sales bar rocketing upward while the bank-balance line dives below zero, meeting at an unpaid wage envelope.
mood: Sobering, practical, protective of small businesses.
pacing: Personal open, one clean contrast, escalation to the shop, hard landing on the final line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and forecast both — earnings and cash.
